situation: You condition an image model on text alone and expect the same face every time.
finding: Diffusion and flow-matching models sample a different point of the learned distribution for every noise initialisation; the report puts text-only facial and structural consistency at roughly 30 to 50 percent.
best_move: Constrain the denoising path with a weight-space adapter (LoRA), a reference adapter (identity embedding injected by cross-attention), or an in-context editing model; treat the text prompt as the weakest lock.
why: The sampler is built for variance, not for tracking an object across calls.
avoid: Relying on a detailed prompt, a locked seed or an agent rule as the identity lock.
caveat: The 30 to 50 percent figure is the report's summary of blog measurements, not a controlled benchmark.

situation: You must pick between Textual Inversion, DreamBooth and LoRA for a character.
finding: All three share one training loop and differ only in which parameters receive gradients: a single token vector (TI, kilobytes, low capacity), the whole U-Net (DreamBooth, gigabytes, prone to language drift and background memorisation without prior preservation), or low-rank matrices on attention projections (LoRA, megabytes). The report's DreamBench figures put DreamBooth above TI on subject fidelity and LoRA close behind at a fraction of the size.
best_move: Default to DreamBooth-LoRA for a flagship character; keep TI for style tokens, not faces; use full fine-tuning only when you can afford prior-preservation data and one checkpoint per character.
why: Capacity scales with trainable parameters; portability and composability scale inversely.
avoid: Training a full checkpoint per character and then trying to merge two of them.
caveat: DreamBench numbers are quoted by the report from secondary sources; the DreamBooth paper is verified, its specific scores here are not.

situation: You fine-tune a whole backbone on three to five photos and the model forgets the class or bakes in the background.
finding: Full fine-tuning on a handful of images induces language drift (the class noun loses its meaning) and context memorisation (training backgrounds and lighting fuse with the identity).
best_move: Train with a class-specific prior-preservation loss on the model's own class generations, or move the update into a LoRA.
why: Every weight is free to move, so the few training images dominate what the class token means.
avoid: Skipping regularisation because the first samples look right.
caveat: Mechanism and remedy are from the DreamBooth line of work; magnitudes depend on the base model.

situation: You want a LoRA for a character on a diffusion-transformer base and need starting hyperparameters.
finding: The report's practitioner consensus for FLUX-class models: 15 to 30 curated references at the model's native resolution, learning rate around 1e-4, batch 1 to 2, rank around 16, about 40 steps per image (roughly 1,000 to 1,400 steps), reaching a 90 to 95 percent consistency ceiling; targeting selected transformer blocks cuts adapter size without losing identity.
best_move: Start there, hold out prompts that change pose and outfit, and stop when held-out identity plateaus rather than when training loss does.
why: Low rank and few steps limit how much the adapter can memorise beyond the face.
avoid: Training on one pose and one outfit; the adapter will reproduce them.
caveat: Blog-sourced recipe; no controlled comparison behind the exact numbers.

situation: Training a dedicated adapter for every minor character is too slow and too heavy.
finding: Zero-shot reference adapters extract an identity embedding from one or a few images at inference and inject it, so a side character needs no training; the report cites a 600-panel comparison where a hybrid zero-shot stack beat per-character LoRAs on pass rate (85 vs 78 percent) with zero onboarding time, while flagship characters still gained the last points from a LoRA on top.
best_move: Tier your cast: zero-shot stack for episodic characters, zero-shot plus LoRA for protagonists.
why: The adapter reads identity features at test time instead of writing them into weights.
avoid: One method for the whole cast.
caveat: HyperDreamBooth confirms the cost argument for per-subject fine-tuning; the 600-panel pass rates come from a single practitioner write-up.

situation: You need an identity adapter that keeps the face without wrecking the scene's lighting and style.
finding: PuLID is a tuning-free identity method that adds a contrastive alignment loss and an accurate ID loss so the inserted face minimally disrupts the base model while keeping identity fidelity high.
best_move: Prefer a contrastively aligned adapter when prompts carry lighting, style or composition you must keep; pair it with a spatial adapter only where head pose is extreme.
why: The adapter is trained to leave everything but the face alone.
avoid: Pushing adapter weight up until the background and palette start copying the reference.
caveat: Verified against the paper's abstract; the report's DivID-120 scores are figures in the source and were not transcribed.

situation: You chose a keypoint-conditioned identity adapter and get rigid poses, colour burn-in or drift at high guidance.
finding: The report lists three production artifacts for keypoint-locked adapters: the face is pinned to the keypoint layout, saturation and contrast burn in at standard guidance scales, and identity drifts when guidance pulls toward the text.
best_move: Cap guidance or restrict the adapter to inpainting passes; supply keypoints that match the target head angle; terminate the adapter early in the schedule.
why: Spatial conditioning and biometric conditioning compete with the text at high guidance.
avoid: Raising guidance to fix a weak prompt while the identity adapter is active.
caveat: Practitioner reports; the adapter's own paper does not frame these as failure modes.

situation: Face adapters leave the body, clothes and height to the text prompt.
finding: Face-centric adapters crop tightly around the head, so torso and extremities are governed only by text; full-body customisation models exist that capture body structure from a single image.
best_move: Lock wardrobe and body separately (try-on pass, pose skeleton, full-body model) instead of expecting a face adapter to hold them.
why: The adapter's input never saw the body.
avoid: Blaming the face adapter for a changed jacket.
caveat: Visual Persona's abstract supports the full-body gap; which tool wins is project-specific.

situation: You rely on one frontal reference and the character turns away from the camera.
finding: Face-recognition features degrade sharply under large pose variation; single-reference adapters then snap the head back toward the camera or invent an off-model profile.
best_move: Average embeddings from several angles, or use a pose-adaptive or 3D-conditioned identity model for profile and steep-angle shots.
why: Self-occlusion hides half the landmarks the embedding depends on.
avoid: Generating a profile shot from the same frontal reference and trusting the similarity score.
caveat: PoseFace verifies the recognition drop under pose; the exact yaw thresholds in the report are secondary.

situation: Faces in wide shots come out melted even with a strong adapter.
finding: The report attributes this to the VAE's fixed spatial downsampling: any feature smaller than one latent cell is destroyed before the first denoising step, so a small face in a wide frame cannot carry identity.
best_move: Render the layout, then crop the face in pixel space, upscale, inpaint with the identity adapter, and composite back; never upscale in latent space for this.
why: The identity tokens have nothing spatial to attach to at that scale.
avoid: Adding more adapter weight to a wide shot.
caveat: Mechanism follows from how latent diffusion encodes images; the pixel thresholds are the report's arithmetic on specific models.

situation: Changing a character's expression with an identity adapter either flattens the emotion or warps the face.
finding: The reference image's expression is entangled in the identity embedding; identity weight and emotion compete, and uniform injection also leaks identity features into backgrounds and lighting. Spatially adaptive injection schedules the face only where and when it forms.
best_move: Build an expression sheet from the master with a dedicated expression tool, and use spatially adaptive or masked injection for prompts that change emotion.
why: One vector carries both who the person is and how they looked that day.
avoid: Asking the prompt for a scream while the adapter holds a smile at full weight.
caveat: SpatialID's abstract verifies the leakage problem and a training-free remedy; the expression-sheet workflow is practitioner guidance.

situation: Few-shot personalisation makes the subject faithful but the prompts stop working.
finding: Fine-tuning on few images trades target fidelity against the model's broad knowledge (text editability); sampling guidance can steer that trade-off at inference.
best_move: Hold out editability prompts in every evaluation of a character adapter, and treat the fidelity-editability dial as a per-shot setting.
why: The adapter moves the model toward the training images and away from everything else.
avoid: Measuring only face similarity.
caveat: Verified against the paper's abstract; the report does not quote its numbers.

situation: You work in a closed image tool with a character-reference parameter and the character still changes.
finding: The report describes the reference weight as a feature-inclusion dial (face only at the low end, face plus hair plus full costume at the top) and names prompt-reference contradiction (text re-describing features the reference already fixes) as the main failure; newer versions generalise references to props and objects but allow one reference per generation.
best_move: Set the weight for what must stay (face only, or face and costume), and strip from the prompt every feature the reference already carries.
why: Two conditioning sources that disagree produce a hybrid.
avoid: Writing 'blue eyes' under a brown-eyed reference.
caveat: Parameter semantics come from vendor documentation and community write-ups; they change between versions.

situation: You iterate on a character over many turns in a conversational image model.
finding: Autoregressive image generation conditions on the whole conversation, so earlier props, lighting and seating positions resurface and identity drifts within a few turns; iterative editors also lose detail through repeated encode-decode passes.
best_move: Branch every new panel from the immutable master reference (one hop from ground truth), decompose edits into atomic steps, and audit early batches for defaults the reference smuggled in.
why: Each turn re-encodes the last output and the whole context, compounding error.
avoid: Chaining edit on edit on edit.
caveat: Mechanisms are plausible and widely reported; no controlled measurement is cited.

situation: You want one model for both generating and editing while keeping the character.
finding: In-context flow-matching editors concatenate the reference image's tokens with the instruction, handling local edits and generation in one architecture; the report warns that quality degrades when many edits are chained linearly.
best_move: Use an in-context editor for single-turn changes from the master; return to the master for the next change rather than editing the edit.
why: The reference is in the context for that call only; the next call's reference is whatever you pass.
avoid: Treating the last output as the new reference by default.
caveat: Architecture verified against the model report's abstract; the degradation-over-turns claim is from the report's reading of it.

situation: Clothing details mutate between panels even when the face holds.
finding: Dedicated virtual try-on networks treat the garment as an image condition: concatenating person and garment latents in one network transfers structure and graphics without extra encoders, and the report lists alternatives that trade speed for fabric fidelity.
best_move: Lock wardrobe with a try-on pass from a canonical flat-lay or on-model garment image; keep the garment asset in the registry next to the face cards.
why: The garment becomes an input image instead of a description.
avoid: Describing a jacket's stitching in words and hoping.
caveat: CatVTON's claim that extra encoders are unnecessary is verified; latency and VRAM numbers are the report's.

situation: Small marks, scars, glasses and props vanish or warp across generations.
finding: Generic prompts regress toward a symmetrical airbrushed mean; small anchors survive only when the master is cast at high resolution with named asymmetries and micro-details, and occluding accessories need an inpainting-capable identity method rather than a face swapper.
best_move: Cast the master at 2K with named asymmetries and one asymmetric tracking prop; use fill-based identity transfer for occluders; use a wearable try-on tool for small accessories.
why: Features need enough pixels to survive encoding and enough specificity to be reproduced.
avoid: 'An imperfect face' as the whole instruction.
caveat: Practitioner guidance; the tool comparisons are from community evaluations.

situation: Two characters in one frame merge heights, swap attributes or lose their phenotypes.
finding: Global text conditioning bleeds across the canvas (spatial bleed), modifiers drift between nouns inside the encoder (attribute bleed), and face datasets' demographic skew lowers baseline fidelity for under-represented phenotypes.
best_move: Isolate each character's prompt to a region, bind modifiers to their nouns before routing, drive heights with a pose skeleton, and choose identity models trained on diverse data.
why: One attention context serves the whole canvas unless you partition it.
avoid: A single prompt sentence for two people.
caveat: The dataset-bias premise is verified; the regional-conditioning recipe is practitioner guidance for one toolkit.

situation: Dramatic poses and camera angles cost you the face.
finding: Posture and identity compete for attention; the report's benchmark moved pose into a skeleton control and split identity tokens into early text-encoder layers, raising dramatic-angle consistency from 71 to 83 percent, with control guidance terminated early so the adapter governs the last steps.
best_move: Externalise pose to a control map, keep the face region out of edge and depth maps, and end control guidance before the final steps.
why: Skeleton input carries geometry the text no longer has to.
avoid: Full-weight edge control over the face through the whole schedule.
caveat: Numbers from one practitioner's 600-panel run; mechanism is sound.

situation: You are starting a character and want the assets production will depend on.
finding: The report's asset-bible sequence: a 2K casting pass (A-pose, neutral backdrop, named asymmetries), a 6-card set derived from it (three full-body, three face angles), an 8-view turnaround audited against seven horizontal guide lines, and a deterministic expression sheet; characters are then tiered by screen time into LoRA-trained or zero-shot registration.
best_move: Build the bible before the first scene and register every card path in the character registry.
why: Everything later conditions on these files; fixing them later means re-rendering.
avoid: Casting in a scene instead of a studio setup.
caveat: A synthesised procedure; individual steps are common practice, the exact audit is the report's.

situation: You lock the seed and expect the same character.
finding: The seed only fixes the initial noise; changing the prompt deflects the trajectory and changing canvas size changes the noise layout, so seed continuity is not identity continuity. Changing only the seed can itself change faithfulness and composition widely.
best_move: Use the seed for reproducibility of one exact call; lock identity with an adapter or a reference, and keep canvas dimensions constant within a sequence.
why: Noise is the starting point, not the destination.
avoid: Reusing a portrait seed on a different aspect ratio.
caveat: Seed sensitivity verified; the step-window and seed-shaping details are from the report.

situation: You wonder which denoising steps actually set the identity.
finding: A step-sweep cited by the report shows identity similarity rising fast in an early window and peaking around step 8 on a 28-step schedule, with later steps refining texture and slightly eroding identity under prolonged guidance.
best_move: Put identity conditioning strongest early; consider distilled few-step backbones for identity work.
why: Low-frequency structure, including the face, forms first.
avoid: Assuming more steps mean more identity.
caveat: Single benchmark quoted by the report; values are model-specific.

situation: You want faster identity-conditioned generation.
finding: A frozen identity adapter trained on a many-step base transfers to the distilled few-step variant without retraining; the report adds that identity similarity held or improved because the short trajectory ends inside the identity window.
best_move: Try the distilled backbone with the same adapter and guidance off before buying more compute.
why: The adapter conditions the same architecture; the schedule is what changed.
avoid: Retraining the adapter for the distilled model by reflex.
caveat: Transfer-without-retraining is verified; the similarity-improvement figures are the report's.

situation: Composited characters look pasted onto their backgrounds.
finding: Three subsystems address it in the report: pixel-space face detailing per detected face (sorted and routed per character), gradient-aware soft inpainting that feathers mask edges into the schedule, and physics-based relighting of the cutout to the plate.
best_move: Detail faces in pixel space, inpaint with a feathered mask, relight the composite; route each face to its own character.
why: Hard masks, latent upscaling and mismatched light are each visible seams.
avoid: One detailer pass that writes the same face onto every body.
caveat: Tool-specific recipe; the principles generalise.

situation: A character adapter breaks after a base-model or sampler change.
finding: Adapters and embeddings are coupled to the weights they were trained against; stochastic and ancestral samplers inject fresh noise each step and never converge, while deterministic solvers reproduce a face as steps increase; the scheduler shifts where in the schedule adapters bite.
best_move: Pin base model, VAE, sampler and scheduler in the registry per character and treat any change as a re-qualification.
why: The adapter is a delta on a specific geometry; the sampler decides whether the path is repeatable.
avoid: Switching to an ancestral sampler for 'more variety' on a locked character.
caveat: Solver determinism is standard; per-scheduler effects on adapters are practitioner observations.

situation: Dense scene descriptions push the character out of the prompt.
finding: Text encoders with a 77-token window and causal attention weight early tokens most and drop what falls past the window; reordering the same description changes the face. The report's fix is an immutable six-slot character prefix at the start of every prompt (age, gender, hair colour, hair style, skin detail, outfit), which in its 600-panel run raised pass rate from 84 to 87.5 percent and cut hair-colour drift from 9 to 2 per 100 panels.
best_move: Compile the character prefix from the registry in fixed slot order at position zero; put scene and action after it.
why: Position and order are part of the conditioning.
avoid: Writing the environment first and the character last.
caveat: Window mechanics are architectural facts; the pass-rate numbers are one practitioner's.

situation: Writers hand-type prompts and every panel describes the character differently.
finding: The report's upstream design: a declarative character registry (typed schema, pinned prefix, anatomical metrics, adapter bindings, reference card paths, wardrobe variants, forbidden defaults, negative rules, gate thresholds) and scripts that reference characters by symbolic id; a deterministic compiler expands ids into the pinned prefix, strips names, budgets tokens, binds colours to garments, and picks the angle-matched reference card.
best_move: Treat the registry as the single source of truth and generate prompts from it; names never appear in prompts.
why: Entropy enters where humans retype what a file already states.
avoid: Keeping character descriptions as prose documents.
caveat: A design synthesis; it matches this repository's registry and token resolution and is the basis for its prompt-compiler guidance.

situation: You need to catch drifted panels without a human looking at each one.
finding: The report's three-gate pipeline: a face-embedding cosine check against the angle-matched reference with pass, warn (auto-detail) and reject (re-seed) bands; a full-body structural check with a self-supervised vision transformer plus a text-alignment score; and a vision-language judge auditing garment attributes, routing failures to repair passes.
best_move: Gate every output automatically against the recorded anchor; wire failures back into regeneration rather than into a review queue.
why: Embedding metrics catch the face and the silhouette; a judge catches semantic garment breaks they miss.
avoid: A single similarity threshold as the whole QA.
caveat: Thresholds (for example 0.60 face cosine) are the report's suggested values, not validated constants.

situation: Your QA passes faces but misses wrong bodies, pets and missing actions.
finding: A face check inspects only the face crop; the report prefers a self-supervised vision transformer over a CLIP image score for full-body gating because it discriminates fine structure between similar characters.
best_move: Add a full-character crop check against the turnaround sheet after the face gate.
why: Different encoders see different things.
avoid: Reusing the face metric for the body.
caveat: Preference is reasoned from the encoders' training objectives; no benchmark is quoted.

situation: Embedding metrics say the jacket matches and it visibly does not.
finding: Numeric similarity metrics cluster in a narrow band and miss localised garment changes (a new zipper, a lost pocket); a vision-language judge prompted with a fixed garment-attribute rubric reportedly agrees with human raters far better than caption-based screening.
best_move: Use a judge model with an attribute rubric for garments and route failures to a try-on repair pass.
why: The judge reasons about parts; the embedding averages them away.
avoid: Trusting a high aggregate similarity for wardrobe.
caveat: The cited evaluation was not verified here; agreement figures are in the source's figures.

situation: You need consistent characters across a long story without training.
finding: Training-free story methods refine each image against the whole set iteratively, or settle identity before rendering so cost does not grow with story length; the report's story benchmark ranks a pre-render identity settlement method highest on cross-frame consistency.
best_move: For long sequences, settle identity once (an anchor) and condition every frame on it rather than on neighbouring frames.
why: Frame-to-frame conditioning compounds error and couples memory to length.
avoid: Chaining panels so each conditions on the previous.
caveat: Both methods' claims verified against their abstracts; the benchmark ranking is the report's table.

situation: You want a pure face identity foundation rather than an adapter on a text model.
finding: An identity-conditioned face foundation model generates diverse photo-realistic images from a face-recognition embedding with higher face similarity than adapter approaches, at the cost of text-driven styling.
best_move: Use it for reference cards, expression sheets and biometric anchors; use adapters for styled scenes.
why: It optimises identity alone.
avoid: Expecting it to follow a scene prompt.
caveat: Verified against the paper's abstract.

situation: You consider zero-shot identity tools and wonder what they need.
finding: Zero-shot identity methods extract identity from a single portrait with a facial encoder and generate in one pass, unlike multi-image fine-tuning.
best_move: One good reference card per angle is the input; invest in those cards.
why: The encoder does the work the fine-tuning used to do.
avoid: Feeding a low-resolution crop as the only reference.
caveat: Verified against the paper's abstract (a paper about protecting against these methods, which describes them accurately).

situation: You hear a latent-space adapter can bridge different model families' latents.
finding: The report claims a latent upscaler adapter can map between 4-channel and 16-channel latent spaces; the verified abstract frames that adapter as latent super-resolution before decoding, not as a cross-family bridge.
best_move: Do not plan a cross-family latent bridge on this claim without reading the full paper; move adapters by retraining or by zero-shot methods.
why: Latent spaces of different VAEs are different coordinate systems.
avoid: Loading a 4-channel latent or adapter into a 16-channel model.
caveat: Status caution: the report's claim goes beyond what the source's abstract states.

situation: You rely on licensed face-analysis weights inside a commercial pipeline.
finding: The report flags that common face-analysis backbones behind several adapters are distributed under non-commercial research terms and names permissively licensed alternatives.
best_move: Record the licence of every identity backbone in the registry binding and choose permissive weights for commercial work.
why: A pipeline inherits the most restrictive licence in it.
avoid: Discovering the licence after launch.
caveat: Licence terms change; verify at the source before relying on this.
